metadata.title: The Geometry of Meaning
metadata.purpose: STEM & AI Architecture, Week 1 — vector embeddings as geometry: tokenization, n-dimensional mapping, cosine distance, a worked 2-D plot, and the antonym flaw that shows where the spatial framework breaks.

beats.narration_text: I am Onkar Bhujbal, a software engineer. How does a computer know that subtracting a man from a king and adding a woman equals a queen? It doesn't read. It does geometry. Today we are looking at vector embeddings — the mathematical foundation of all modern A.I.

beats.honesty_note: king - man + woman ≈ queen is the canonical word2vec demonstration and is the source script's own example. Shown as the illustration it is, not as a live model run; no model or version is named.

beats.narration_text: A model has no idea what a word means. It knows where that word sits relative to every other word. Meaning, to a machine, is a position in space — and distance is the whole trick.

beats.narration_text: We understand language A.I. through the Spatial Distance Framework. One: turn words into numerical tokens. Two: map those numbers onto a multi-dimensional coordinate graph. Three: measure the angle between those coordinates using cosine distance. Words with similar meanings cluster together in space.
beats.new_visual_element: The Spatial Distance Framework — three stages, lit in narration order

stages.name: N-DIMENSIONAL MAPPING

beats.narration_text: So let's collapse those hundreds of dimensions down to just two, and plot something we can actually look at — three words, one graph, and a distance we can measure by eye.
beats.new_visual_element: Ask micro-beat — the generation prompt for the 2-D plot

running indicator reads 'plotting the space…'; no output lines — the next beat IS the output

props.command: Plot DOG, WOLF and CAT on two axes — domestication against canine traits — and measure the distance between them.

beats.authoring_note: ASK → RESULT pair: B03 is the ask, B04 is the result (ASK→RESULT LAW).

beats.narration_text: Let's apply the framework to a simplified two-D model. If our X axis is domestication and our Y axis is canine traits, dog sits top right. Wolf sits top left — high canine, low domestic. Cat sits bottom right. The A.I. doesn't know what a dog is. It knows the distance from dog to wolf is shorter than the distance to a car.
beats.new_visual_element: The 2-D semantic space — three points and one measured distance

CAT snaps in bottom right

beats.honesty_note: Axis ENDS are labelled to match the script's own coordinates and VO: the script writes the X axis as 'DOMESTIC <-> WILD' but gives DOG x=+0.8 and WOLF x=-0.9 and says dog sits RIGHT — so +x is DOMESTIC. Labelling it the script's way round would contradict the plotted points. Coordinates are the script's, and the card says on screen that this is a simplified 2-D teaching model, not real embedding output.

beats.narration_text: So where does this spatial framework break? Antonyms. Ask an embedding model to plot hot and cold, and it puts them almost on top of each other. Why? Because they appear in the exact same sentence structures. The coffee is hot. The coffee is cold. Without explicit logical guardrails, vector math confuses opposites for synonyms.
beats.new_visual_element: The antonym flaw — two opposite words, nearly identical vectors

'hot' and 'cold' both light terracotta — the ONLY difference between the two sentences
terracotta verdict block drops: THE ANTONYM FLAW

props.sparkLine: Close in space. Opposite in meaning.
props.simCaption: identical context, opposite meaning — the vectors barely move
props.verdictSub: vector math reads opposites as synonyms without explicit logical guardrails

beats.honesty_note: 0.82 is the SOURCE SCRIPT'S stated figure, shown because the author put it on screen — it is illustrative of the effect, not a measurement this build ran. Logged in SOURCES.md. The bar fills to 0.82 so the number and the graphic agree.

beats.narration_text: So don't take my word for it. Run this exact Python script to calculate the cosine similarity between two opposite coordinates. You'll see exactly how mathematical distance turns into a relationship.

show.event: code card opens on a hard cut; traffic-light dot arms terracotta
the script reveals line by line as the voice describes it
the expected result lands as a comment: -1.0, perfectly opposed

props.title: cosine.py
props.code:
import numpy as np

a = [1, 0]
b = [-1, 0]

print(np.dot(a, b) / (np.linalg.norm(a) * np.linalg.norm(b)))

# -> -1.0
#
# Perfectly opposed vectors score -1.
# Now try it on real embeddings for
# "hot" and "cold" and watch it fail.

beats.honesty_note: -1.0 is arithmetic, not a claim: cosine of [1,0] and [-1,0] is exactly -1. Verified rather than asserted. The closing comment is the reel's addition — it connects the toy result back to the antonym flaw, which is the point of running it.

beats.narration_text: And when that toy example works, here's the prompt worth running. Ask a model for ten pairs of words it would place close together that actually mean opposite things, and make it explain what the two words share. What comes back is a map of where geometry stops being meaning — written by the thing that uses it.
beats.new_visual_element: Handoff — the viewer's prompt, read aloud

props.command: Give me 10 pairs of words an embedding model would place CLOSE together that actually mean OPPOSITE things. For each pair, explain what context the two words share that pulls them together.

beats.narration_text: A machine doesn't read meaning. It measures distance — and most of the time, that is close enough to look like understanding. Onkar Bhujbal, for Humanitarians AI.
